lessons.title: The Credit Cycle Turn: When Bank Lending Signals a Bottom

body.text: The credit cycle bottoms only after banks have recognised and provided for the bad loans of the last downturn, not the moment growth stops decelerating. That balance-sheet clean-up, more than any single growth number, is the actual signal of a genuine credit-driven recovery.

children.text: Lesson 3.3 covered credit growth composition as a recession gauge. This lesson covers the other side of the same data: what it actually takes for the credit cycle to turn, and why that turn, unlike credit growth's deceleration on the way into a slowdown, tends to be a genuinely lagging confirmation rather than an early signal.
Why Credit Is Structurally the Last Piece to Turn

markDefs.definition: A loan on which the borrower has stopped making scheduled interest or principal payments for a specified period, requiring the bank to set aside provisions against likely losses and disclose it as impaired on its balance sheet.

children.text: There is a real asymmetry worth internalising here. Credit growth decelerating is a genuinely leading recession signal, per Lesson 3.3, because banks pull back lending in anticipation of stress. But credit growth reaccelerating is not an equally leading recovery signal, because banks first have to work through the

built up during the downturn before they can lend freely again. Recognising a loan as non-performing, provisioning against it, and either recovering or writing it off, all takes time, often several years, and banks with weak capital positions or large unprovided NPAs remain cautious lenders long after the real economy has technically started to recover. This is why the credit cycle turn, as opposed to a temporary stabilisation in credit growth, tends to arrive later than most of the other early-cycle recovery signals from Lesson 4.1.
The Markers of a Genuine Credit Cycle Bottom

body.caption: What to check before calling a genuine credit cycle turn

cells: The banking system's stock of bad loans peaking and actually declining, not just new NPA formation slowing
A slower pace of new bad loans still leaves the existing overhang weighing on lending capacity
Provisioning expense as a share of loans normalising back toward its long-run average
High credit costs continue suppressing bank profitability and risk appetite even after growth data has turned
Bank capital ratios stabilising or improving, often after recapitalisation
Undercapitalised banks are structurally constrained from expanding lending, regardless of demand
Credit growth broadening across ratings and across long-term project finance, not just short-term working capital or retail
Concentrated growth in the safest, shortest-tenor lending reflects caution, not genuine confidence returning

children.text: IBC and the Resolution Mechanism: India's Specific Wrinkle

markDefs.definition: A framework enacted in 2016 that created a formal, time-bound legal process for resolving corporate insolvency in India, either through a restructuring plan approved by creditors or through liquidation, replacing a patchwork of slower, less predictable mechanisms that existed before it.

children.text: India's credit cycle carries a specific structural wrinkle worth knowing: the

, enacted in 2016, gave banks a formal, comparatively faster route to resolve or recover stressed corporate loans than existed before it, even though actual resolutions have often taken longer than the statute's own timelines in practice. A wave of large IBC resolutions through the following years was a meaningful part of clearing what analysts often called India's twin balance sheet problem, over-leveraged corporates and undercapitalised, stressed public sector banks, an overhang that had suppressed credit growth for years after the 2011-13 slowdown covered in Lesson 1.1. Watching IBC resolution volumes and recovery rates is a genuinely useful, India-specific supplement to the standard NPA and credit cost markers above.

body.label: Indian Banking System Gross NPA Ratio (Illustrative Trajectory)
body.value: Peaked around 11% (FY18), declined to low single digits over following years
body.context: Widely reported approximate figures from RBI Financial Stability Reports; the multi-year decline reflects recognition, provisioning, and IBC-driven resolution working through the system, not a quick reversal. Always check the RBI's current Financial Stability Report for exact figures.

children.text: Distinguishing a Genuine Turn From a Dead-Cat Bounce

A temporary uptick in credit growth is not automatically a genuine cycle turn. If the pickup is concentrated in short-term working capital or in retail and personal loans alone, the late-cycle masking pattern flagged in Lesson 3.3, it may simply reflect banks staying cautious while still extending the safest, shortest-duration credit available. A genuine turn looks different: growth broadening into longer-term project finance and industrial credit, which signals businesses are making multi-year capacity decisions again, not just managing near-term cash flow. This is the same discipline this course has applied repeatedly, checking composition, not just the aggregate number, applied one more time to the specific question of whether a credit recovery is real.

body.text: Do not treat credit growth symmetrically across the cycle. Its deceleration is a genuinely leading recession signal, but its reacceleration is a comparatively lagging recovery signal, delayed by however long it takes banks to recognise, provision for, and resolve the prior downturn's bad loans. Confusing the two directions' timing is a common and costly mistake.

body.title: Confirming a Genuine Credit Cycle Turn
steps: Check whether the banking system's Gross NPA ratio is actually declining, not just whether new NPA formation has slowed
Check whether credit cost (provisioning as a share of loans) is normalising back toward its long-run average
Check bank capital adequacy ratios for signs of stabilisation or recapitalisation
Check whether credit growth is broadening into long-term project finance and industrial lending, not just short-term or retail credit
Where relevant, check IBC resolution volumes and recovery rates as a supplementary, India-specific signal of how much of the prior downturn's bad-debt overhang has actually cleared

body.title: Real Turn or Dead-Cat Bounce?
body.scenario: Non-food credit growth has picked up from 5% to 9% over the last two quarters. Digging deeper, this pickup is almost entirely in retail personal loans and short-term working capital lending; long-term project finance to industry is still contracting. The banking system's Gross NPA ratio has stopped rising but has not yet declined from its peak, and two large state-run banks are still operating under RBI's Prompt Corrective Action framework, which restricts their lending.
body.prompt: Is this a genuine credit cycle turn by this lesson's framework, or something narrower? What is the strongest evidence either way?
body.modelAnswer: This looks more like a narrow stabilisation than a genuine credit cycle turn. The growth pickup is concentrated in retail and short-term working capital, exactly the composition pattern this lesson flags as insufficient on its own, while long-term project finance, the marker most indicative of businesses making genuine multi-year confidence decisions, is still contracting. The NPA ratio has only stopped rising, not actually declined, meaning the bad-debt overhang from the prior downturn is still largely unresolved. Two banks still under Prompt Corrective Action is direct evidence of ongoing capital and lending constraints at the institutional level, reinforcing that the banking system as a whole is not yet in a position to lend broadly and confidently. The strongest evidence against calling this a genuine turn is the combination of a still-elevated NPA ratio and contracting long-term project finance; both would need to reverse before this qualifies as more than a partial, retail-led stabilisation.

body.title: Check Your Understanding
body.question: Why is credit growth reaccelerating not treated as an equally leading signal as credit growth decelerating, within this course's framework?
options: Because credit growth data is only published during a slowdown, not during a recovery

Because banks must first recognise, provision for, and resolve the prior downturn's bad loans before they can lend broadly again, which introduces a structural lag on the way back up that does not exist on the way down
Because the RBI stops publishing Sectoral Deployment of Credit data during a recovery
Because retail credit growth is always fraudulent during a recovery
body.explanation: Credit deceleration reflects banks pulling back quickly in anticipation of stress, a fast, forward-looking reaction. Credit reacceleration is slowed by the time it takes to work through NPA recognition, provisioning, and resolution from the prior downturn, which is exactly why this lesson treats the credit cycle turn as a comparatively lagging recovery confirmation rather than an early signal.

body.text: This lesson presents a general framework for reading the credit cycle, for educational purposes. NPA and credit cost figures cited are widely reported approximations, not precise current data; always check the RBI's Financial Stability Report and individual bank disclosures for current figures. Nothing here is investment advice.

points: Credit growth deceleration is a leading recession signal, but credit growth reacceleration is a comparatively lagging recovery signal, delayed by the time banks need to recognise, provision, and resolve prior bad loans

A genuine credit cycle bottom shows a declining Gross NPA ratio, normalising credit costs, stabilising bank capital, and broadening credit growth into long-term project finance, not just retail or short-term lending

India's IBC framework, enacted in 2016, gave banks a faster formal resolution route and was a meaningful part of clearing the twin balance sheet problem that suppressed credit growth for years after the 2011-13 slowdown
A credit growth pickup concentrated in retail and short-term working capital alone is not sufficient evidence of a genuine turn; check composition the same way Lesson 3.3 taught for the downturn side
The next lesson closes Chapter 4 by covering the false recovery signals that most often trip up this entire framework
